description: Hi, I’m Liyan, a computer science student from Bangladesh interested in space science, game development and AI. I build games in C++ and OpenGL, and for this challenge I built Space Mission, a 5-level educational space shooter based on real NASA asteroid missions (Bennu, Apophis, Psyche, Dimorphos, Arrokoth). I ported it to run in the browser using WebAssembly and added an AI Astronomer that explains each discovery and answers players’ questions.
summary:
Astra-Strike is a free browser-based educational space shooter that teaches players about real NASA asteroids and missions. Players fly through five levels of increasing difficulty, fighting enemy ships and using power-ups such as shields. In the later levels they discover real space objects, including Bennu, Apophis, Psyche, Dimorphos and Arrokoth. Each discovery unlocks a verified fact from NASA missions such as OSIRIS-REx, DART and Psyche, and is saved in a discovery log. An AI Astronomer, powered by Claude, explains each object in simple language and answers the player’s questions.

It addresses the challenge by turning real mission science into an experience students can play instead of read. This matters because asteroids and planetary defense are exciting but hard to learn from textbooks. Because the game runs in any modern browser from a link, with no install, it is easy to share with students anywhere.
details:
Astra-Strike is a free browser-based educational space shooter in five levels. The player flies a spacecraft, dodges and shoots enemy ships, and collects power-ups such as shields. Score and lives carry over between levels, and the difficulty rises as the game goes on. Each level starts with a mission briefing. In the later levels the player discovers real space objects (Bennu, Apophis, Psyche, Dimorphos, Arrokoth). Each discovery unlocks a short NASA fact and is saved in a discovery log. A final screen shows the result and high score.

An AI Astronomer panel sits next to the game. When an object is discovered, it explains it in simple language and answers follow-up questions such as “Why does it matter for Earth?” or “Explain it like I’m 10.” It uses Claude from Anthropic, with the verified fact from the game included as context. If the AI is unavailable, the panel falls back to the built-in NASA facts, so the game always works.

Benefits

  • Students learn real asteroid science by playing instead of reading.
  • It opens from a link in any modern browser, with no install and no cost.
  • The AI panel lets players follow their own curiosity at their own pace.

Intended impact
To make asteroid science and planetary defense approachable and fun for students, especially those who find textbooks dry. Because the game is shareable by link, teachers and students can use it anywhere, including on low-end computers.

Tools, languages and software

  • C++ and OpenGL (freeglut) for the game
  • Emscripten, to compile the game to WebAssembly so it runs in the browser
  • HTML and JavaScript for the web page and the AI panel
  • Anthropic Claude API for the AI Astronomer, through a small Cloudflare Worker proxy that keeps the API key off the player’s device
  • Code::Blocks and VS Code for development; GitHub Pages for hosting
  • No special hardware; any device with a modern browser

How it is creative
It combines an arcade game with real mission data, so the facts are rewards for playing, not homework. The AI Astronomer turns a one-way fact into a conversation. The game was originally a desktop C++ program, and we brought it to the web so anyone can play it from a link.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA/JPL pages [list sources you checked], and the AI prompt tells the model to say when it is unsure instead of guessing.
  • Reliability: an offline fallback means the game never breaks if the AI is down.
  • Security and privacy: the API key is kept on a server proxy, and no personal data is collected.
  • Accessibility: plays in the browser with no install, using simple keyboard controls.
  • Audience: short, simple explanations written for students.
